<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[co:commons:Category:Makimuku Site]][[en:Makimuku ruins]][[ja:纒向遺跡]][[zh:缠向遗址]] <!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[co:commons:Category:Makimuku Site]][[en:Makimuku ruins]][[ja:纒向遺跡]][[zh:缠向遗址]] <!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[sn:commons:Category:Makimuku Site]][[en:Makimuku ruins]][[ja:纒向遺跡]][[zh:缠向遗址]]
{{Short description|Ruins in Japan}} {{Use dmy dates|date=November 2024}} {{more citations needed|date=February 2022}}
[[File:Makimuku_Site,_tatemonogun.jpg|right|thumb|300x300px|Makimuku ruins Tsuji district]] {{coord|34|32|45.81|N|135|50|24.71|E|region:JP-29_type:landmark|display=title|name=纒向遺跡}} {{Location map|Japan|width=240|caption=Location of the Makimuku ruins in Japan|label=Makimuku ruins|position=bottom|mark=Red pog.svg|marksize=10|lat_deg=34|lat_min=32|lat_sec=45.81|lon_deg=135|lon_min=50|lon_sec=27.71}}
The '''Makimuku ruins''' are ruins in {{ill|Nara Prefecture|en|Nara Prefecture|WD=Q131287|lt=Nara Prefecture|1=Nara Prefecture}} {{ill|Sakurai, Nara|en|Sakurai, Nara|WD=Q127026|lt=Sakurai|1=Sakurai, Nara}}<ref>{{Cite web|title=「鎌倉」でなく「北条時代」が区切り 時代区分に新提案：朝日新聞デジタル|url=https://www.asahi.com/articles/ASKB05T40KB0ULZU015.html|access-date=2022-01-02|website=朝日新聞デジタル|language=ja}}</ref> near {{ill|Mount Miwa|en|Mount Miwa|WD=Q860627|lt=Mount Miwa|1=Mount Miwa}}. Recovered artifacts are of the [[:en:Yayoi Period|Yayoi Period]] and [[:en:Kofun Period|Kofun Period]].
It is designated as a national historic site, and an archaeological site that began in the 3rd century, and some researchers consider the area to be the birthplace of the {{ill|Kofun system|en|Kofun system|WD=Q11397224|lt=Kofun system|1=Keyhole tomb order}}. There is a theory that they are the center of {{ill|Yamatai|en|Yamatai|WD=Q844295|lt=Yamatai country|1=Yamatai}}, and six ancient Kofuns such as {{ill|Hashihaka Kofun|en|Hashihaka Kofun|WD=Q11603420|lt=Hashihaka Kofun|1=Hashihaka Kofun}} are distributed.
== Location and site outline == [[File:Makimuku_Ruins_(Tsuji_area)-3.jpg|link=https://ja.Wikipedia.org/wiki/%E3%83%95%E3%82%A1%E3%82%A4%E3%83%AB:Makimuku_Ruins_(Tsuji_area)-3.jpg|right|thumb|240x240px|Tsuji District, distant viewJR {{ill|Sakurai Line|en|Sakurai Line|WD=Q865801|lt=Sakurai Line|1=Sakurai Line}} {{ill|Makimuku Station|en|Makimuku Station|WD=Q4980794|lt=Makimuku Station|1=Makimuku Station}} at the back of the building remains. To the rear left is {{ill|Mount Miwa|en|Mount Miwa|WD=Q860627|lt=Mount Miwa|1=Mount Miwa}} and to the far right is the {{ill|Hashihaka Kofun|en|Hashihaka Kofun|WD=Q11603420|lt=Hashihaka Kofun|1=Hashihaka Kofun}}.]] The name of the {{ill|Archaeological site|en|Archaeological site|WD=Q839954|lt=Archaeological site|1=Archaeological site}} comes from the village of Makimuku in the former {{ill|Shiki District, Nara|en|Shiki District, Nara|WD=Q1155036|lt=Isogi-gun|1=Shiki District, Nara}}, and the village name "Makimuku" was taken from the "Makimuku Tamaki Palace" of {{ill|Emperor Suinin|en|Emperor Suinin|WD=Q314850|lt=Suinin|1=Emperor Suinin}} and the "Makimuku Hijiro Palace" of {{ill|Emperor Keikō|en|Emperor Keikō|WD=Q329723|lt=Emperor Keikō|1=Emperor Keikō}}'s "Tamaki Palace" and Emperor Hishiro Palace of {{ill|Emperor Keikō|en|Emperor Keikō|WD=Q329723|lt=Keikō|1=Emperor Keikō}}, {{efn|{{ill|Bungo-kuni-fudoki|en|Bungo-kuni-fudoki|WD=Q11633698|lt=Bungo-kuni-fudoki|1=Bungo no Kuni Fudoki}}[https://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/2541894/4], which is named after the ancient story of "Gōu {{ill|Emperor Keikō|en|Emperor Keikō|WD=Q329723|lt=Emperor Keikō|1=Emperor Keikō}}, conqueror of [[Kumaso|Kumano]], who is said to have left Chikugo Province on the occasion of the triumphal return of [[Kumaso]]. It is said to have been the site of the first battle between the two emperors.}}
As of 2011, the area of the site is known as the Karasuda River in the north, the Gomihara River in the south, the Makinochi area bordering the Yamanobe Road in the east, and the Higashida area in the west, which covers an area of about 3 square kilometers. On the map of the site, the area of the site is centered on JR Makimuki Station and stretches about 2 km from east to west and about 1.5 km from north to south, forming an oval shape with an area of 3 square kilometers.
The {{ill|terrain|en|terrain|WD=Q186131|lt=terrain|1=Terrain}} is high in the east and low in the west. The streams of {{ill|Mount Miwa|en|Mount Miwa|WD=Q860627|lt=Mount Miwa|1=Mount Miwa}}, Makimukyamata and Anashiyama join the Makimuku River, and archaeological sites are formed on its {{ill|Alluvial fan|en|Alluvial fan|WD=Q465088|lt=Alluvial fan|1=Alluvial fan}}. It has been confirmed that there was damage caused by a mudslide during the [[:en:Jomon|Jomon period]]. Perhaps because of this, no [[:en:Yayoi Period|Yayoi Period]] {{ill|Human settlement|en|Human settlement|WD=Q486972|lt=settlements|1=Human settlement}} or {{ill|Moat|en|Moat|WD=Q88480|lt=Moat|1=Moat}}s have been detected at the site. Only fragments of ''{{ill|Dōtaku|en|Dōtaku|WD=Q2312868|lt=Dōtaku|1=Dōtaku}}'' and two {{ill|Prehistoric storage pits|en|Prehistoric storage pits|WD=Q1421012|lt=earthen mines|1=Prehistoric storage pits}} have been found. A short distance to the south of the site, a large number of pottery shards dating to the middle and late Yayoi period have been excavated, as well as square moated tomb and {{ill|Pit-house|en|Pit-house|WD=Q940435|lt=pit dwelling|1=Pit-house}}. Also, many Yayoi period artifacts have been excavated from the southwest side. However, {{ill|Yayoi pottery|en|Yayoi pottery|WD=Q11487461|lt=Yayoi earthenware|1=Yayoi pottery}} of the late Kinai V style has been found in the northern lower layer of the north ditch and the gray clay layer of the site, and it is classified as "Garengi 1" in "Garengi chronology".<ref name="ishino2" /> Note that [[Archaeological excavation|excavation]], who was in charge of the [[:ja:石野博信|Ishino Hironobu]], assigned the calendar years 180 to 210 for "Garment 1".
The site is considered by some researchers to be the best candidate for the [[:en:Kofun Period|Kofun Period]], as it shows the transition from the Yayoi period to the [[:en:Kofun Period|Kofun Period]], and may be the site that proves the {{ill|Yamatai Honshu Theory|en|Yamatai Honshu Theory|WD=Q11643036|lt=Yamatai Honshu Theory|1=Yamatai Honshu Theory}}. In 2011, a part of another large building was found about 5 meters to the east of the large building ruins, and the building ruins may have been built in the late 3rd century or later.<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20120627155838/http://www.sankei-kansai.com/2011/04/28/20110428-052260.php 2011th year 4月28日産経新聞関西「大和政権の重要施設か、纒向遺跡で新たな大型建物跡」] 2019th year 8月14日archive差し替え・閲覧</ref>。
A {{ill|Kibi Province|en|Kibi Province|WD=Q1155128|lt=Kibi|1=Kingdom of Kibi}}-type ritual relic, the komon enban, has been excavated from the moat around the Ishizuka tumulus. At the end of the 4th century, after the peak, {{ill|Haniwa|en|Haniwa|WD=Q849376|lt=Haniwa|1=Haniwa}} were excavated.
From the {{ill|Asuka period|en|Asuka period|WD=Q210688|lt=Asuka period|1=Asuka period}} to the {{ill|Nara period|en|Nara period|WD=Q189178|lt=Nara period|1=Nara period}}, a city developed in this area and was called "Oichi". This is why the Hashihaka Tomb is referred to as "Oichi Tomb" in the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|en|Imperial Household Agency|WD=Q1143602|lt=Imperial Household Agency|1=Imperial Household Agency}} ruling. From the Nara period to the {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period|1=Heian period}}, the remains of wells, earthen defences and old river channels have been found. Pottery with {{ill|ink-painted pottery|ja|墨書土器|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/ink-painted pottery|1=ink-inscribed pottery|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11429419}} and the word "Oichi" has also been found.
The remains were designated a national historic site on 17 October {{ill|2013|en|2013|WD=Q1998|lt=2013|1=2013}} (Heisei 25) as the "Makimuku Site".<ref name="国指定">[https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/401/00003818 纒向遺跡] – 国指定文化財等データベース（[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]]</ref>。
== Excavations == [[File:Pottery_from_Makimuku_archaeological_site.jpg|link=https://ja.Wikipedia.org/wiki/%E3%83%95%E3%82%A1%E3%82%A4%E3%83%AB:Pottery_from_Makimuku_archaeological_site.jpg|right|thumb|240x240px|burial goods from the early Kofun period excavated in the 174th survey (2012). Sakurai City Archaeological Center Exhibition]] The site of Makimuku was first introduced by Minoru Doi in 1937 as the "Ohta Site" in "Yamato Shi".<ref name="ishino2">{{Cite book|author=石野, 博信|url=http://worldcat.org/oclc/675187978|title=邪馬台国の候補地・纒向遺跡|date=2008|publisher=Shinsensha|isbn=978-4-7877-0931-8|oclc=675187978}}</ref>。Before it was called by its present name, it was known to the academic world as the "Ota Site" and "Katsuyama Site", and was recognized by researchers as one of a group of small {{ill|archaeological site|en|archaeological site|WD=Q839954|lt=site|1=Archaeological site}}s, and did not attract any particular attention<ref>[[Shunkichi Matsumoto]] in his "History of Omiwa Town" (1959), and [[Shunji Kojima]] in his " Archaeology of Nara Prefecture" (1965), and [[Kojima Shunji]] gave only a summary.</ref>。However, a plan to build prefectural housing and a primary school to promote the employment of coal mine leavers was brought up, which led to a preliminary survey by {{ill|The Museum, Archaeological Institute of Kashihara, Nara Prefecture|en|The Museum, Archaeological Institute of Kashihara, Nara Prefecture|WD=Q112961122|lt=Archaeological Institute of Kashihara|1=The Museum, Archaeological Institute of Kashihara, Nara Prefecture}} to carry out a preliminary survey. As a result, a canal-like structure with a width of 5m, a depth of 1m, and a total length of more than 200m was found, and local Man'yōshū researcher Yoshinobu Yoshioka and others suggested that it might be the remains of the Makimukugawa River, which appears in {{ill|Man'yōshū|en|Man'yōshū|WD=Q834321|lt=Man'yōshū|1=Man'yōshū}}.<ref name="ishino2" />。From the remains of the river, special vessel bases were excavated, which have been found at the Kibi Tate Tsuki and Miyakizaka sites. After the fifteenth survey in 1977, the research was transferred from the Archaeological Institute of Kashihara to the {{ill|Sakurai, Nara|en|Sakurai, Nara|WD=Q127026|lt=Sakurai|1=Sakurai, Nara}} As of December 2008, only 5% of the site had been excavated.<ref name="ishino2" />。
In 2009 (Heisei 21), several Buildings were detected, and it has become clear that the site seems to be part of a City surrounded by {{ill|Fortification|en|Fortification|WD=Q57821|lt=Fortification|1=Fortification}}s.
On 17 September 2010, the Board of Education of Sakurai City, Nara Prefecture, announced that about 2,000 seeds of {{ill|Peach|en|Peach|WD=Q13189|lt=la|1=Peach}} {{ill|peach|en|peach|WD=Q13189|lt=peach|1=Peach}} were found in an oval-shaped "clay pit" (4.3 meters north–south, 2.2 meters east–west, 80 centimeters deep) dug in the 3rd century, about 4 meters south of the remains of a large building. {{ill|Peach|en|Peach|WD=Q13189|lt=Peach|1=Peach}} seeds were found. Peach seeds are used as offerings in ancient rituals and are often found in Yayoi period ruins, but this is the largest number of seeds unearthed in one place in Japan.<ref>2010th year 9月17日日本経済新聞 [https://web.archive.org/web/20180522045912/https://www.nikkei.com/article/DGXNASHC1701V_X10C10A9000000/ 「奈良・纒向遺跡で大量の桃の種、邪馬台国の有力地2000個超、祭祀に使用か」] 2021st year 8月27日閲覧</ref>。In 2011, more than six types of fish bones and scales were found at the site, including {{ill|Pagrus major|en|Pagrus major|WD=Q1196387|lt=Madai|1=Pagrus major}}, {{ill|Caranginae|en|Caranginae|WD=Q64869235|lt=Horsefish|1=Caranginae}}, [[Mackerel]] and {{ill|Common carp|en|Common carp|WD=Q81110|lt=Common carp|1=Common carp}}. They also announced that they had found over a thousand animal bones, including those of {{ill|Wild boar|en|Wild boar|WD=Q58697|lt=Wild boar|1=Wild boar}}s, {{ill|Deer|en|Deer|WD=Q23390|lt=Deer|1=Deer}}s and Ducks.
=== Main Detected Remains === It is about 10 times larger than the Karako-Kagi site and larger than the {{ill|Taga Castle|en|Taga Castle|WD=Q870867|lt=Taga Castle|1=Taga Castle}} site, which was a major military base in the Tohoku region.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://www.worldcat.org/oclc/37459785|title=Taikei Nihon no rekishi|date=1992–1993|publisher=Shōgakkan|others=Makoto Sahara, 佐原眞|isbn=4-09-461001-4|edition=Shohan|location=Tōkyō|oclc=37459785}}</ref>。There are also traces of urban planning throughout the site. [[File:Three Makimuku kofun aerial view.jpg|link=https://ja.Wikipedia.org/wiki/%E3%83%95%E3%82%A1%E3%82%A4%E3%83%AB:Three Makimuku kofun aerial view.jpg|thumb|240x240px|The three tumuli are surrounded by the Makimuku Katsuyama tumulus (top), the Yatsuka tumulus (bottom left) and the Ishizuka tumulus (bottom right), and the Makimuku Elementary School is located between them.]]
* Two huge linear {{ill|waterway|en|waterway|WD=Q1267889|lt=waterway|1=Waterway}}s, 5m wide and 1m deep, revetted with sheet piles and known as the "North Ditch" and "South Ditch".
:* South ditch: extends from the Makimuki River near the tip of the protruding part of the Hashihaka Tomb tomb in a northwesterly direction towards the present-day Garoshi Elementary School. The source of the water is the circumference moat of the Hashihaka Tomb. Behind the moat is the Kunizu Shrine, which reaches the present-day Makimuki River. :* North Ditch: extends from the former Anashi River in the north-east towards the south-west. The source of the water is the old Makimuki River. : The confluence of the two ditches is located on the grounds of the Makimuku Elementary School, and is estimated to be 2,600m long. It connects with the {{ill|Yamato River|en|Yamato River|WD=Q9001527|lt=Yamato River|1=Yamato River}}, which in turn connects to the distant open sea.
* {{ill|Spring (hydrology)|en|Spring (hydrology)|WD=Q124714|lt=Spring water|1=Spring (hydrology)}} was found at the bottom, and the interior is divided into three main layers. About 150 irregularly shaped circular pits with one side protruding, about 3m in diameter and 1.5m deep, were found. * The remains of dugout pillar buildings and the remains of accompanying buildings (a building of the first half of the Kofun period with a floor space of about 23 m<sup>2</sup> in 2×3 rooms, the remains of a collapsed house and wooden products with black lacquered arcs, a small house of 1×1 rooms and a total pillar building of 2×2 rooms and wooden products with black lacquered arcs, a stone monument of the former site of the Tamaki Palace in Tamaki, and the existence of a palace residence are suspected. In addition, 17 dugout pillar buildings were found.) * {{ill|Pit-house|en|Pit-house|WD=Q940435|lt=Pit-house|1=Pit-house}}
: However, there were not many pit dwellings, and it is likely that the buildings were built on stilts.<ref name="ishino2" />。
* V-shaped compartmental ditch with arcaded panels, earthworks and fence rows * Remains of a water-conducting facility (possibly a palace drainage facility) * {{ill|Festival|en|Festival|WD=Q132241|lt=Ritual|1=Festival}} site (a jasper jade, a cusp, a tubular jade, a small glass jade, and pottery from the second half of the 4th century were excavated from the traditional site of Emperor Keiko's palace in Anashi-Doyodo district) * Iron-making site – {{ill|Metalsmith|en|Metalsmith|WD=Q838566|lt=Metalsmith|1=Metalsmith}} site with {{ill|Tsukushi Province|en|Tsukushi Province|WD=Q1206461|lt=Tsukushi|1=Tsukushi Province}}-shaped blowpipe. It is estimated to date from the late 4th century, when iron was smelted in the Kinai region. * Fences around the settlement. * Ancient Kofuns scattered around the site (Makimuku Kofun Group)
There is also the possibility that many buried tombs, which cannot be seen above ground, are buried underground.<gallery> File:Makimuku Site, Tatemono-B.jpg|Tsuji Area Building B File:Makimuku Site, Tatemono-C.jpg|Tsuji Area Building C File:Makimuku Site, Tatemono-D.jpg|Tsuji Area Building D </gallery>
=== Main excavated artifacts ===
* {{ill|Earthenware|en|Earthenware|WD=Q1377111|lt=Earthenware|1=Earthenware}}s from the late [[:en:Yayoi Period|Yayoi Period]] to the early [[:en:Kofun Period|Kofun Period]] were excavated, and the {{ill|Yayoi pottery|en|Yayoi pottery|WD=Q11487461|lt=Yayoi potteries|1=Yayoi pottery}} and {{ill|Haji pottery|en|Haji pottery|WD=Q5639938|lt=Haji pottery|1=Haji pottery}}. According to them, the five periods are Yayoi pottery style V (Makimuku 1), Shonai pottery (Makimuku 2, Makimuku 3 and Makimuku 4) and Nururu I (Makimuku 5). However, the dates are based on the C14 dating method, which may be more than 100 years old. * Vermilion-painted chicken-shaped wooden product * A wooden product known as an 'arc-shaped circular plate', with a design combining straight and curved lines, believed to have its origins in the Kibi region. * Drawstring bag made of silk However, silk was not produced in the Kinai region until the 4th century. * Tiled earthenware (Pottery fragments were excavated in 1996 (Heisei 8). Analyses of the composition of the clay components confirmed in 2001 that the pottery was unique in Japan, and that it was made using techniques from the {{ill|Korea|en|Korea|WD=Q18097|lt=Korea|1=Korea}}. * A miniature boat * Wooden arrowheads * Iwami-type shield-shaped wooden wares * a large number of imported pottery (exotic pottery).
However, there is a lack of conclusive evidence to date the site, such as the absence of bronze mirrors, swords, jade beads and iron objects, so it is not possible to say definitively that this was the site of the Yamatai Kingdom. {| cellpadding="0" border="0" style="float:right; border:2px solid #cccfff" |+'''Proportion of the area of origin of the pottery brought in''' |Ise and Tokai region !49% |- |Hokuriku and San-in region !17% |- |Kawachi region !10% |- |Kibi region !7% |- |Omi region !5% |- |Kanto region !5% |- |Harima region !3% |- |Western Seto Inland Sea region !3% |- |Kii region !1% |}
{{ill|Artifact (archaeology)|en|Artifact (archaeology)|WD=Q220659|lt=burial goods|1=Artifact (archaeology)}} have been unearthed from all over Japan, but most of them were made in {{ill|Ise Province|en|Ise Province|WD=Q864166|lt=Ise Province|1=Ise Province}}, which is adjacent to {{ill|Yamato Province|en|Yamato Province|WD=Q907495|lt=Yamato Province|1=Yamato Province}} and has had a close relationship with the country since ancient times. {{ill|Ise Province|en|Ise Province|WD=Q864166|lt=Ise Province|1=Ise Province}}, which was adjacent to {{ill|Yamato Province|en|Yamato Province|WD=Q907495|lt=Yamato Province|1=Yamato Province}} and had close relations with {{ill|Ise Bay|en|Ise Bay|WD=Q1368308|lt=Ise Bay|1=Ise Bay}}, and {{ill|Owari Province|en|Owari Province|WD=Q514506|lt=Owari Province|1=Owari Province}}, which is located to the east across {{ill|Ise Bay|en|Ise Bay|WD=Q1368308|lt=Ise Bay|1=Ise Bay}}. In addition to the pottery brought in, there is a large amount of pottery that was made in Yamato but is said to have regional characteristics, and the proportion of such pottery is higher at {{ill|Festival|en|Festival|WD=Q132241|lt=Ritual|1=Festival}}-related sites (30% of all pottery excavated at many sites). In addition, although these exotic pottery and artifacts are found from [[Kyushu]] to {{ill|Kantō region|en|Kantō region|WD=Q132480|lt=Kanto|1=Kantō region}} and the {{ill|Sea of Japan|en|Sea of Japan|WD=Q27092|lt=Sea of Japan|1=Sea of Japan}} side, there is very little pottery of Kyushu or Korean origin, suggesting that this site had little trade with the continent.<ref name="ishino2" /><ref name="tera2" /><gallery> File:纒向遺跡出土 土器群.JPG| part_of of excavated earthenware </gallery>
=== The main tombs of the Makimuku site ===
* [[Makimuku Ishizuka Kofun]] * {{ill|Makimuku Katsuyama Kofun|en|Makimuku Katsuyama Kofun|WD=Q11608502|lt=Makimuku Katsuyama Kofun|1=Makimuku Katsuyama Kofun}} * {{ill|Makimuku Yazuka Kofun|en|Makimuku Yazuka Kofun|WD=Q11608503|lt=Makimuku Yazuka Kofun|1=Makimuku Yatsuka Kofun}} * {{ill|Higashida Ōtsuka Kofun|en|Higashida Ōtsuka Kofun|WD=Q11528075|lt=Higaida-ōtsuka Kofun|1=Higaida Ōtsuka Kofun}} * [[Hokenoyama Kofun]] * {{ill|Hashihaka Kofun|en|Hashihaka Kofun|WD=Q11603420|lt=Hashihaka Kofun|1=Hashihaka Kofun}} === A peculiar site ===
* Although the site is said to be a large settlement, the remains of an inhabited settlement have not been found. All that can be seen today are ritual buildings, earthen mounds, ritual implements such as arcane discs and chicken-shaped wooden products, and large and small ditches (canals) protected by cypress sheet piles for distribution. Many scholars believe that the site was not a residential area, but rather a place for frequent gatherings of people and goods, and for rituals to {{ill|Mount Miwa|en|Mount Miwa|WD=Q860627|lt=Mount Miwa|1=Mount Miwa}} around the {{ill|Hashihaka Kofun|en|Hashihaka Kofun|WD=Q11603420|lt=Hashihaka Kofun|1=Hashihaka Kofun}}. * In the Tsuji/Torii-mae area, a 2 × 3 m long {{ill|Post in ground|en|Post in ground|WD=Q1695743|lt=digout pillar building|1=Post in ground}} and a row of fences running east–west to the south of it have been found; in the Ota Minami Tobizuka area, the remains of a collapsed house have been found; and in the Makinochi Ietsura area, a small 1 × 1 m long house and a 2 × 2 m long building with full columns have been found. In addition, 17 dugout pillar buildings have been found in the Ota Meguri area, and pit dwelling remains have been found in the Higashida Kakinoki and Ota Tobizuka areas. * According to Hironobu Ishino, this is "a large settlement site that suddenly appeared at the end of the 2nd century and suddenly disappeared in the middle of the 4th century".<ref name="ishino2" />。
=== Excavation Report ===
* [[:ja:石野博信|Ishino Hironobu]], [[:ja:関川尚功|Sekikawa Naokoh]], "Garments," Sakurai City Board of Education, September 1976. * [[:ja:関川尚功|Sekikawa, Naokoh]] and Matsunaga, Hiroaki, "Summary of Excavations at the Garoshi Site," The Archaeological Institute of Kashihara, 1984. * Naokoh Sekikawa and Hiroaki Matsunaga, "An Overview of the Excavation of the Garoshi Archaeological Site," The Archaeological Institute of Kashihara, Nara Prefecture, 1985. * [https://sitereports.nabunken.go.jp/62709 "Report on the Excavation of the Makimuku Site", Sakurai Municipal Archaeological Center, Excavation Report 28, 2007]. * [https://sitereports.nabunken.go.jp/62743 "Makimuku Ruins", Sakurai City Board of Education, Education Division, 1981]. * [https://sitereports.nabunken.go.jp/ja/53677 "Sakurai City Excavation Report by the National Treasury Subsidy in 2015", Sakurai Municipal Archaeological Heritage Excavation Report 46, 2017].
== Characteristics of the site ==
* The site dates from the late Yayoi period to the early {{ill|Kofun period|en|Kofun period|WD=Q459939|lt=Kofun period|1=Kofun period}}. * It is one of the largest settlement sites of its time, covering a vast area. * The {{ill|Hashihaka Kofun|en|Hashihaka Kofun|WD=Q11603420|lt=Hashihaka Kofun|1=Hashihaka Kofun}}, which has {{ill|Folklore|en|Folklore|WD=Q36192|lt=Tradition|1=Folklore}} as the tomb of [[Himiko]], is a huge 280-metre-long mound. The preceding mound, the Makimuku-type post-frontal-yen mound, with a mound length of around 90 m, is also the largest mound in the Japanese archipelago in the 3rd century, and is the first great royal tomb of the [[:en:Yamato Kingdom|Yamato Kingship]]. It is thought that the two tombs were politically linked, as they were also built in other parts of Japan. * {{ill|Himiko|en|Himiko|WD=Q234451|lt=Himiko|1=Himiko}}, the queen of the Yamataikoku Kingdom, according to one theory.
: Kazuo Higo introduces the view of Shinya Kasai in the {{ill|Taishō era|en|Taishō era|WD=Q329174|lt=Taisho|1=Taishō era}} period.<ref>{{Cite web|title=肥後和男『邪馬台国は大和である (1971st year )』 – 邪馬台国畿内説 卑弥呼はヤマトトモモソヒメ|url=https://www.buccyake-kojiki.com/archives/1016925732.html|access-date=2022-02-01|website=神社と古事記|language=ja}}</ref>。According to it, Kasai assigned Himiko to Momosohime, and her brother {{ill|Emperor Sujin|en|Emperor Sujin|WD=Q333530|lt=Emperor Sujin|1=Emperor Sujin}} to {{ill|Emperor Sujin|en|Emperor Sujin|WD=Q333530|lt=Emperor Sujin|1=Emperor Sujin}}. The rationale for this is as follows. :# Emperor Sujin's year of death in the Chinese zodiac was Boshin, close to the year of Himiko's death. :# It is clear that Himiko was a kind of priestess from the legend of her marriage to the deity of Mt. Miwa, and from the story of Nichiya Hitosaku, Yaya Kamisaku. She was the aunt of Emperor Sojin, but from the point of view of a foreigner (Chen Shou), she could be forgiven for being as wrong as his nephew and brother.
: Although there are many skeptics of this theory, some archaeologists believe that it is not unnatural for the Hashihaka Tomb to be Himiko's tomb, as the oldest giant anterior-posterior mound is the Hashihaka Tomb (the view of Shiraishi Taichiro and others).<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Shiraishi|first1=Taichirō|url=https://www.worldcat.org/oclc/45330682|title=Kofun to yamato seiken : kodai kokka wa ikani keisei sareta ka|last2=白石太一郎|date=1999|publisher=Bungei Shunjū|isbn=4-16-660036-2|location=Tōkyō|oclc=45330682}}</ref>。On the other hand, the size of the posterior circle of the {{ill|Hashihaka Kofun|en|Hashihaka Kofun|WD=Q11603420|lt=Hashihaka Kofun|1=Hashihaka Kofun}}, which is about 160m in diameter, may not match the description of Himiko's tomb in the {{ill|Wajinden|en|Wajinden|WD=Q1135798|lt=Wajinden|1=Wajinden}}. It is written in {{ill|Wajinden|en|Wajinden|WD=Q1135798|lt=Wajinden|1=Wajinden}} that "Heimyako died in a large tomb, which is about a hundred paces away from the tomb", which means that the size of the tomb is about 30m in the case of the short ri used in {{ill|Wajinden|en|Wajinden|WD=Q1135798|lt=Wajinden|1=Wajinden}}, which means that the Hashihaka Tomb is too big. Furthermore, the size of the Kofun was described in terms of diameter in the Wei Shi Wajin Den, so it is thought to be a round Kofun or similar. Therefore, there is a question mark over the use of the Hashihaka Tomb as the tomb of Himiko. (However, there is a theory that the front part of the tomb was additionally constructed in later times.)
* In 2013, more than 100 postholes were found in a building that is believed to have been constructed in the 3rd century. It is thought that the building was built and demolished many times.<ref>[http://sankei.jp.msn.com/life/news/130202/art13020213480002-n1.htm 卑弥呼の祭祀用建物跡？奈良・纒向遺跡で柱穴１００個超出土] 産経新聞 2013rd year 2月2日</ref>。 * Although pottery was brought in throughout the 3rd century, about 15% of the total excavated {{ill|pottery|en|pottery|WD=Q11642|lt=earthenware|1=Pottery}} is made up of pottery brought in from Suruga, Owari, Ise, Omi, Hokuriku, San'in, Kibi and other areas, but there is little pottery from northern Kyushu. The proportion of ritual-related remains is about 30%, but there are very few bronze mirrors and swords, which indicate exchange with the continent. This suggests that at that time there was a local royal power in this area which had little to do with Kitakyushu or the continent. * There are no Han mirrors, later Han mirrors or swords found at this site to prove that Himiko {{ill|Cao Wei|en|Cao Wei|WD=Q320930|lt=Cao Wei|1=Cao Wei}} and others interacted with the continent. In addition, no iron arrowheads were excavated. According to [[:ja:関川尚功|Sekikawa Naokoh]], "According to the Book of Wei, Himiko frequently sent messengers to Wei, and from Wei also came messengers and soldiers, so there was active exchange with the peninsula and the continent. Therefore, the active exchange with the peninsula and Korea as shown in the Heian-period Japanese history has not been proven and the site is not the site of the {{ill|Yamatai|en|Yamatai|WD=Q844295|lt=Yamatai|1=Yamatai}}.<ref>財団法人古代学協会、関川尚功（せきがわ ひさよし）邪馬台国と箸墓古墳</ref>。
=== The Royal Capital of the Yamato Kingdom === Kaoru Terasawa, in his book "The Birth of the Yamato Kingdom: The Royal Capital, the Makimuku Site and its Kofun Tombs", lists six features and peculiarities of the Makimuku Site<ref name="tera2">{{Cite book|url=https://www.worldcat.org/oclc/74978499|title=Nihon no kōkogaku : Doitsu ten kinen gaisetsu = Japans Archäologie und Geschichte bis zu den ersten Kaisern|version=2006 printing |publisher=Gakuseisha|others=Takashi Inada, 稲田孝司, Nara Bunkazai Kenkyūjo, 奈良文化財研究所.|isbn=4-311-75034-X|location=Tōkyō|oclc=74978499}}</ref>。
# It appeared suddenly at the beginning of the 3rd century. It is a very well planned settlement and large in size. # The site is the largest in the Japanese archipelago and had a municipal function. The site was the largest in the Japanese archipelago and had a municipal function. # There are few domestic utensils and civil engineering tools are conspicuous, and a huge canal was built and large-scale civil engineering works for city construction were carried out. # Water-conducting facilities and ritual facilities are royal rituals. Royalty-related buildings. Arcuate designs originating from the royal tombs of Kibi, special vessel bases and jars. # The {{ill|Hashihaka Kofun|en|Hashihaka Kofun|WD=Q11603420|lt=Hashihaka Kofun|1=Hashihaka Kofun}}, which was stylised on the edge of the habitation space, and the garnet-shaped posterior frontal Kofun that preceded it. # Ironware production. (No ironware has been found at the Garoshi site).
In addition, there is a pottery with "Oichi" written in ink from the early Heian period, and this site is considered to correspond to the "Ohoichi" township described in "[[Wamyō Ruijushō]]". '''{{ill|Shinto texts|en|Shinto texts|WD=Q11588760|lt=Kiki|1=Shinto texts}}'''", it is known that the city had a municipal function until later times, and furthermore, the {{ill|Emperor Suinin|en|Emperor Suinin|WD=Q314850|lt=Emperor Suinin|1=Emperor Suinin}} and {{ill|Emperor Keikō|en|Emperor Keikō|WD=Q329723|lt=Emperor Keikō|1=Emperor Keikō}}'s Shiki-no-mizukaki-no-miya, {{ill|Emperor Suinin|en|Emperor Suinin|WD=Q314850|lt=Emperor Suinin|1=Emperor Suinin}}, and {{ill|Emperor Keikō|en|Emperor Keikō|WD=Q329723|lt=Tamaki-no-Hishiro-no-Miya|1=Emperor Keikō}}, {{ill|Folklore|en|Folklore|WD=Q36192|lt=Folklore|1=Folklore}} are described as having existed.<ref name="tera2" />。
After saying this, Terasawa concluded, "There is no other huge settlement in the Japanese archipelago in the third century that has such a total of archaeological and philological features. Therefore, it is highly probable that the third-century site of Gengen was the city where the capital palace of the first kingship of the archipelago, called the {{ill|Yamato Kingship|en|Yamato Kingship|WD=Q2658252|lt=Yamato Kingdom|1=Yamato Kingship}}, was located".
Hironobu Ishino also argues that it was not a naturally occurring village but an artificially built city, based on the discovery of a large ditch and a ritual site with a seawall leading to the Yamato River, the unusually large number of pottery artifacts from outside the Kinki region, and the fact that at least one out of every five people at Gengen is estimated to have come from outside the Yamato region.<ref name="ishino2" />。
The following remarks also reinforce the view that the site is the birthplace of the {{ill|Yamato Kingship|en|Yamato Kingship|WD=Q2658252|lt=Yamato Kingship|1=Yamato Kingship}} or the royal capital of the {{ill|Yamato Kingship|en|Yamato Kingship|WD=Q2658252|lt=Yamato Kingship|1=Yamato Kingship}}.
* In the surrounding area, there are also palaces such as Nagase Asakura Palace of {{ill|Emperor Yūryaku|en|Emperor Yūryaku|WD=Q357235|lt=Emperor Yūryaku|1=Emperor Yūryaku}} in the 5th century, and Shiki (Isogi) Shima Omiya (Kinshiku) Palace of {{ill|Emperor Kinmei|en|Emperor Kinmei|WD=Q329792|lt=Kinmei|1=Emperor Kinmei}} in the 6th century. * The [[:en:Man'yoshu|Man'yoshu]] also contains many poems about the place name.
=== Birthplace of the Zenpokoenfun === [[File:Hashihaka_kohun_aerial.jpg|link=https://ja.Wikipedia.org/wiki/%E3%83%95%E3%82%A1%E3%82%A4%E3%83%AB:Hashihaka_kohun_aerial.jpg|right|thumb|240x240px|{{ill|Hashihaka Kofun|en|Hashihaka Kofun|WD=Q11603420|lt=Hashihaka Kofun|1=Hashihaka Kofun}}]] The {{ill|Hashihaka Kofun|en|Hashihaka Kofun|WD=Q11603420|lt=Hashihaka Kofun|1=Hashihaka Kofun}} located at the site is generally considered to be the beginning of the stylized {{ill|Kofun system|en|Kofun system|WD=Q11397224|lt=Zenpokoenfun system|1=Keyhole tomb order}}. Kaoru Terasawa considers the tombs belonging to the Makimukushizuka tumulus that preceded the {{ill|Hashihaka Kofun|en|Hashihaka Kofun|WD=Q11603420|lt=Hashihaka Kofun|1=Hashihaka Kofun}}, such as the Makimukushizuka tumulus, using the concept of "Makimukushizuka-type post-frontal-round tumulus", and places them in the emergence-period tumulus<ref>寺沢薫 「纒向型前方後円墳の築造」 同志社大学考古学シリーズIV『考古学と技術』同志社大学考古学シリーズ刊行会、1988th year 。</ref>。
Katsuyama Kofun is a [[scallop-shaped kofun]] with some elements indicating it was tranditional between that type and later {{ill|Zenpokoenfun|en|Zenpokoenfun|WD=Q11268718|lt=Zenpokoenfun|1=Zenpōkōenfun}}.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Kidder |first=J. Edward |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1515/9780824862848 |title=Himiko and Japan's Elusive Chiefdom of Yamatai |date=18 December 2017 |publisher=University of Hawaii Press |isbn=978-0-8248-6284-8}}</ref>{{ill|Zenpokoenfun|en|Zenpokoenfun|WD=Q11268718|lt={{rp|249}}}}
== See also ==

{{Short description|Ruins in Japan}} {{Use dmy dates|date=November 2024}} {{more citations needed|date=February 2022}}
[[File:Makimuku_Site,_tatemonogun.jpg|right|thumb|300x300px|Makimuku ruins Tsuji district]] {{coord|34|32|45.81|N|135|50|24.71|E|region:JP-29_type:landmark|display=title|name=纒向遺跡}} {{Location map|Japan|width=240|caption=Location of the Makimuku ruins in Japan|label=Makimuku ruins|position=bottom|mark=Red pog.svg|marksize=10|lat_deg=34|lat_min=32|lat_sec=45.81|lon_deg=135|lon_min=50|lon_sec=27.71}}
The '''Makimuku ruins''' are ruins in {{ill|Nara Prefecture|en|Nara Prefecture|WD=Q131287|lt=Nara Prefecture|1=Nara Prefecture}} {{ill|Sakurai, Nara|en|Sakurai, Nara|WD=Q127026|lt=Sakurai|1=Sakurai, Nara}}<ref>{{Cite web|title=「鎌倉」でなく「北条時代」が区切り 時代区分に新提案：朝日新聞デジタル|url=https://www.asahi.com/articles/ASKB05T40KB0ULZU015.html|access-date=2022-01-02|website=朝日新聞デジタル|language=ja}}</ref> near {{ill|Mount Miwa|en|Mount Miwa|WD=Q860627|lt=Mount Miwa|1=Mount Miwa}}. Recovered artifacts are of the [[:en:Yayoi Period|Yayoi Period]] and [[:en:Kofun Period|Kofun Period]].
It is designated as a national historic site, and an archaeological site that began in the 3rd century, and some researchers consider the area to be the birthplace of the {{ill|Kofun system|en|Kofun system|WD=Q11397224|lt=Kofun system|1=Keyhole tomb order}}. There is a theory that they are the center of {{ill|Yamatai|en|Yamatai|WD=Q844295|lt=Yamatai country|1=Yamatai}}, and six ancient Kofuns such as {{ill|Hashihaka Kofun|en|Hashihaka Kofun|WD=Q11603420|lt=Hashihaka Kofun|1=Hashihaka Kofun}} are distributed.
== Location and site outline == [[File:Makimuku_Ruins_(Tsuji_area)-3.jpg|link=https://ja.Wikipedia.org/wiki/%E3%83%95%E3%82%A1%E3%82%A4%E3%83%AB:Makimuku_Ruins_(Tsuji_area)-3.jpg|right|thumb|240x240px|Tsuji District, distant viewJR {{ill|Sakurai Line|en|Sakurai Line|WD=Q865801|lt=Sakurai Line|1=Sakurai Line}} {{ill|Makimuku Station|en|Makimuku Station|WD=Q4980794|lt=Makimuku Station|1=Makimuku Station}} at the back of the building remains. To the rear left is {{ill|Mount Miwa|en|Mount Miwa|WD=Q860627|lt=Mount Miwa|1=Mount Miwa}} and to the far right is the {{ill|Hashihaka Kofun|en|Hashihaka Kofun|WD=Q11603420|lt=Hashihaka Kofun|1=Hashihaka Kofun}}.]] The name of the {{ill|Archaeological site|en|Archaeological site|WD=Q839954|lt=Archaeological site|1=Archaeological site}} comes from the village of Makimuku in the former {{ill|Shiki District, Nara|en|Shiki District, Nara|WD=Q1155036|lt=Isogi-gun|1=Shiki District, Nara}}, and the village name "Makimuku" was taken from the "Makimuku Tamaki Palace" of {{ill|Emperor Suinin|en|Emperor Suinin|WD=Q314850|lt=Suinin|1=Emperor Suinin}} and the "Makimuku Hijiro Palace" of {{ill|Emperor Keikō|en|Emperor Keikō|WD=Q329723|lt=Emperor Keikō|1=Emperor Keikō}}'s "Tamaki Palace" and Emperor Hishiro Palace of {{ill|Emperor Keikō|en|Emperor Keikō|WD=Q329723|lt=Keikō|1=Emperor Keikō}}, {{efn|{{ill|Bungo-kuni-fudoki|en|Bungo-kuni-fudoki|WD=Q11633698|lt=Bungo-kuni-fudoki|1=Bungo no Kuni Fudoki}}[https://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/2541894/4], which is named after the ancient story of "Gōu {{ill|Emperor Keikō|en|Emperor Keikō|WD=Q329723|lt=Emperor Keikō|1=Emperor Keikō}}, conqueror of [[Kumaso|Kumano]], who is said to have left Chikugo Province on the occasion of the triumphal return of [[Kumaso]]. It is said to have been the site of the first battle between the two emperors.}}
As of 2011, the area of the site is known as the Karasuda River in the north, the Gomihara River in the south, the Makinochi area bordering the Yamanobe Road in the east, and the Higashida area in the west, which covers an area of about 3 square kilometers. On the map of the site, the area of the site is centered on JR Makimuki Station and stretches about 2 km from east to west and about 1.5 km from north to south, forming an oval shape with an area of 3 square kilometers.
The {{ill|terrain|en|terrain|WD=Q186131|lt=terrain|1=Terrain}} is high in the east and low in the west. The streams of {{ill|Mount Miwa|en|Mount Miwa|WD=Q860627|lt=Mount Miwa|1=Mount Miwa}}, Makimukyamata and Anashiyama join the Makimuku River, and archaeological sites are formed on its {{ill|Alluvial fan|en|Alluvial fan|WD=Q465088|lt=Alluvial fan|1=Alluvial fan}}. It has been confirmed that there was damage caused by a mudslide during the [[:en:Jomon|Jomon period]]. Perhaps because of this, no [[:en:Yayoi Period|Yayoi Period]] {{ill|Human settlement|en|Human settlement|WD=Q486972|lt=settlements|1=Human settlement}} or {{ill|Moat|en|Moat|WD=Q88480|lt=Moat|1=Moat}}s have been detected at the site. Only fragments of ''{{ill|Dōtaku|en|Dōtaku|WD=Q2312868|lt=Dōtaku|1=Dōtaku}}'' and two {{ill|Prehistoric storage pits|en|Prehistoric storage pits|WD=Q1421012|lt=earthen mines|1=Prehistoric storage pits}} have been found. A short distance to the south of the site, a large number of pottery shards dating to the middle and late Yayoi period have been excavated, as well as square moated tomb and {{ill|Pit-house|en|Pit-house|WD=Q940435|lt=pit dwelling|1=Pit-house}}. Also, many Yayoi period artifacts have been excavated from the southwest side. However, {{ill|Yayoi pottery|en|Yayoi pottery|WD=Q11487461|lt=Yayoi earthenware|1=Yayoi pottery}} of the late Kinai V style has been found in the northern lower layer of the north ditch and the gray clay layer of the site, and it is classified as "Garengi 1" in "Garengi chronology".<ref name="ishino2" /> Note that [[Archaeological excavation|excavation]], who was in charge of the [[:ja:石野博信|Ishino Hironobu]], assigned the calendar years 180 to 210 for "Garment 1".
The site is considered by some researchers to be the best candidate for the [[:en:Kofun Period|Kofun Period]], as it shows the transition from the Yayoi period to the [[:en:Kofun Period|Kofun Period]], and may be the site that proves the {{ill|Yamatai Honshu Theory|en|Yamatai Honshu Theory|WD=Q11643036|lt=Yamatai Honshu Theory|1=Yamatai Honshu Theory}}. In 2011, a part of another large building was found about 5 meters to the east of the large building ruins, and the building ruins may have been built in the late 3rd century or later.<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20120627155838/http://www.sankei-kansai.com/2011/04/28/20110428-052260.php 2011th year 4月28日産経新聞関西「大和政権の重要施設か、纒向遺跡で新たな大型建物跡」] 2019th year 8月14日archive差し替え・閲覧</ref>。
A {{ill|Kibi Province|en|Kibi Province|WD=Q1155128|lt=Kibi|1=Kingdom of Kibi}}-type ritual relic, the komon enban, has been excavated from the moat around the Ishizuka tumulus. At the end of the 4th century, after the peak, {{ill|Haniwa|en|Haniwa|WD=Q849376|lt=Haniwa|1=Haniwa}} were excavated.
From the {{ill|Asuka period|en|Asuka period|WD=Q210688|lt=Asuka period|1=Asuka period}} to the {{ill|Nara period|en|Nara period|WD=Q189178|lt=Nara period|1=Nara period}}, a city developed in this area and was called "Oichi". This is why the Hashihaka Tomb is referred to as "Oichi Tomb" in the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|en|Imperial Household Agency|WD=Q1143602|lt=Imperial Household Agency|1=Imperial Household Agency}} ruling. From the Nara period to the {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period|1=Heian period}}, the remains of wells, earthen defences and old river channels have been found. Pottery with {{ill|ink-painted pottery|ja|墨書土器|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/ink-painted pottery|1=ink-inscribed pottery|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11429419}} and the word "Oichi" has also been found.
The remains were designated a national historic site on 17 October {{ill|2013|en|2013|WD=Q1998|lt=2013|1=2013}} (Heisei 25) as the "Makimuku Site".<ref name="国指定">[https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/401/00003818 纒向遺跡] – 国指定文化財等データベース（[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]]</ref>。
== Excavations == [[File:Pottery_from_Makimuku_archaeological_site.jpg|link=https://ja.Wikipedia.org/wiki/%E3%83%95%E3%82%A1%E3%82%A4%E3%83%AB:Pottery_from_Makimuku_archaeological_site.jpg|right|thumb|240x240px|burial goods from the early Kofun period excavated in the 174th survey (2012). Sakurai City Archaeological Center Exhibition]] The site of Makimuku was first introduced by Minoru Doi in 1937 as the "Ohta Site" in "Yamato Shi".<ref name="ishino2">{{Cite book|author=石野, 博信|url=http://worldcat.org/oclc/675187978|title=邪馬台国の候補地・纒向遺跡|date=2008|publisher=Shinsensha|isbn=978-4-7877-0931-8|oclc=675187978}}</ref>。Before it was called by its present name, it was known to the academic world as the "Ota Site" and "Katsuyama Site", and was recognized by researchers as one of a group of small {{ill|archaeological site|en|archaeological site|WD=Q839954|lt=site|1=Archaeological site}}s, and did not attract any particular attention<ref>[[Shunkichi Matsumoto]] in his "History of Omiwa Town" (1959), and [[Shunji Kojima]] in his " Archaeology of Nara Prefecture" (1965), and [[Kojima Shunji]] gave only a summary.</ref>。However, a plan to build prefectural housing and a primary school to promote the employment of coal mine leavers was brought up, which led to a preliminary survey by {{ill|The Museum, Archaeological Institute of Kashihara, Nara Prefecture|en|The Museum, Archaeological Institute of Kashihara, Nara Prefecture|WD=Q112961122|lt=Archaeological Institute of Kashihara|1=The Museum, Archaeological Institute of Kashihara, Nara Prefecture}} to carry out a preliminary survey. As a result, a canal-like structure with a width of 5m, a depth of 1m, and a total length of more than 200m was found, and local Man'yōshū researcher Yoshinobu Yoshioka and others suggested that it might be the remains of the Makimukugawa River, which appears in {{ill|Man'yōshū|en|Man'yōshū|WD=Q834321|lt=Man'yōshū|1=Man'yōshū}}.<ref name="ishino2" />。From the remains of the river, special vessel bases were excavated, which have been found at the Kibi Tate Tsuki and Miyakizaka sites. After the fifteenth survey in 1977, the research was transferred from the Archaeological Institute of Kashihara to the {{ill|Sakurai, Nara|en|Sakurai, Nara|WD=Q127026|lt=Sakurai|1=Sakurai, Nara}} As of December 2008, only 5% of the site had been excavated.<ref name="ishino2" />。
In 2009 (Heisei 21), several Buildings were detected, and it has become clear that the site seems to be part of a City surrounded by {{ill|Fortification|en|Fortification|WD=Q57821|lt=Fortification|1=Fortification}}s.
On 17 September 2010, the Board of Education of Sakurai City, Nara Prefecture, announced that about 2,000 seeds of {{ill|Peach|en|Peach|WD=Q13189|lt=la|1=Peach}} {{ill|peach|en|peach|WD=Q13189|lt=peach|1=Peach}} were found in an oval-shaped "clay pit" (4.3 meters north–south, 2.2 meters east–west, 80 centimeters deep) dug in the 3rd century, about 4 meters south of the remains of a large building. {{ill|Peach|en|Peach|WD=Q13189|lt=Peach|1=Peach}} seeds were found. Peach seeds are used as offerings in ancient rituals and are often found in Yayoi period ruins, but this is the largest number of seeds unearthed in one place in Japan.<ref>2010th year 9月17日日本経済新聞 [https://web.archive.org/web/20180522045912/https://www.nikkei.com/article/DGXNASHC1701V_X10C10A9000000/ 「奈良・纒向遺跡で大量の桃の種、邪馬台国の有力地2000個超、祭祀に使用か」] 2021st year 8月27日閲覧</ref>。In 2011, more than six types of fish bones and scales were found at the site, including {{ill|Pagrus major|en|Pagrus major|WD=Q1196387|lt=Madai|1=Pagrus major}}, {{ill|Caranginae|en|Caranginae|WD=Q64869235|lt=Horsefish|1=Caranginae}}, [[Mackerel]] and {{ill|Common carp|en|Common carp|WD=Q81110|lt=Common carp|1=Common carp}}. They also announced that they had found over a thousand animal bones, including those of {{ill|Wild boar|en|Wild boar|WD=Q58697|lt=Wild boar|1=Wild boar}}s, {{ill|Deer|en|Deer|WD=Q23390|lt=Deer|1=Deer}}s and Ducks.
=== Main Detected Remains === It is about 10 times larger than the Karako-Kagi site and larger than the {{ill|Taga Castle|en|Taga Castle|WD=Q870867|lt=Taga Castle|1=Taga Castle}} site, which was a major military base in the Tohoku region.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://www.worldcat.org/oclc/37459785|title=Taikei Nihon no rekishi|date=1992–1993|publisher=Shōgakkan|others=Makoto Sahara, 佐原眞|isbn=4-09-461001-4|edition=Shohan|location=Tōkyō|oclc=37459785}}</ref>。There are also traces of urban planning throughout the site. [[File:Three Makimuku kofun aerial view.jpg|link=https://ja.Wikipedia.org/wiki/%E3%83%95%E3%82%A1%E3%82%A4%E3%83%AB:Three Makimuku kofun aerial view.jpg|thumb|240x240px|The three tumuli are surrounded by the Makimuku Katsuyama tumulus (top), the Yatsuka tumulus (bottom left) and the Ishizuka tumulus (bottom right), and the Makimuku Elementary School is located between them.]]
* Two huge linear {{ill|waterway|en|waterway|WD=Q1267889|lt=waterway|1=Waterway}}s, 5m wide and 1m deep, revetted with sheet piles and known as the "North Ditch" and "South Ditch".
:* South ditch: extends from the Makimuki River near the tip of the protruding part of the Hashihaka Tomb tomb in a northwesterly direction towards the present-day Garoshi Elementary School. The source of the water is the circumference moat of the Hashihaka Tomb. Behind the moat is the Kunizu Shrine, which reaches the present-day Makimuki River. :* North Ditch: extends from the former Anashi River in the north-east towards the south-west. The source of the water is the old Makimuki River. : The confluence of the two ditches is located on the grounds of the Makimuku Elementary School, and is estimated to be 2,600m long. It connects with the {{ill|Yamato River|en|Yamato River|WD=Q9001527|lt=Yamato River|1=Yamato River}}, which in turn connects to the distant open sea.
* {{ill|Spring (hydrology)|en|Spring (hydrology)|WD=Q124714|lt=Spring water|1=Spring (hydrology)}} was found at the bottom, and the interior is divided into three main layers. About 150 irregularly shaped circular pits with one side protruding, about 3m in diameter and 1.5m deep, were found. * The remains of dugout pillar buildings and the remains of accompanying buildings (a building of the first half of the Kofun period with a floor space of about 23 m<sup>2</sup> in 2×3 rooms, the remains of a collapsed house and wooden products with black lacquered arcs, a small house of 1×1 rooms and a total pillar building of 2×2 rooms and wooden products with black lacquered arcs, a stone monument of the former site of the Tamaki Palace in Tamaki, and the existence of a palace residence are suspected. In addition, 17 dugout pillar buildings were found.) * {{ill|Pit-house|en|Pit-house|WD=Q940435|lt=Pit-house|1=Pit-house}}
: However, there were not many pit dwellings, and it is likely that the buildings were built on stilts.<ref name="ishino2" />。
* V-shaped compartmental ditch with arcaded panels, earthworks and fence rows * Remains of a water-conducting facility (possibly a palace drainage facility) * {{ill|Festival|en|Festival|WD=Q132241|lt=Ritual|1=Festival}} site (a jasper jade, a cusp, a tubular jade, a small glass jade, and pottery from the second half of the 4th century were excavated from the traditional site of Emperor Keiko's palace in Anashi-Doyodo district) * Iron-making site – {{ill|Metalsmith|en|Metalsmith|WD=Q838566|lt=Metalsmith|1=Metalsmith}} site with {{ill|Tsukushi Province|en|Tsukushi Province|WD=Q1206461|lt=Tsukushi|1=Tsukushi Province}}-shaped blowpipe. It is estimated to date from the late 4th century, when iron was smelted in the Kinai region. * Fences around the settlement. * Ancient Kofuns scattered around the site (Makimuku Kofun Group)
There is also the possibility that many buried tombs, which cannot be seen above ground, are buried underground.<gallery> File:Makimuku Site, Tatemono-B.jpg|Tsuji Area Building B File:Makimuku Site, Tatemono-C.jpg|Tsuji Area Building C File:Makimuku Site, Tatemono-D.jpg|Tsuji Area Building D </gallery>
=== Main excavated artifacts ===
* {{ill|Earthenware|en|Earthenware|WD=Q1377111|lt=Earthenware|1=Earthenware}}s from the late [[:en:Yayoi Period|Yayoi Period]] to the early [[:en:Kofun Period|Kofun Period]] were excavated, and the {{ill|Yayoi pottery|en|Yayoi pottery|WD=Q11487461|lt=Yayoi potteries|1=Yayoi pottery}} and {{ill|Haji pottery|en|Haji pottery|WD=Q5639938|lt=Haji pottery|1=Haji pottery}}. According to them, the five periods are Yayoi pottery style V (Makimuku 1), Shonai pottery (Makimuku 2, Makimuku 3 and Makimuku 4) and Nururu I (Makimuku 5). However, the dates are based on the C14 dating method, which may be more than 100 years old. * Vermilion-painted chicken-shaped wooden product * A wooden product known as an 'arc-shaped circular plate', with a design combining straight and curved lines, believed to have its origins in the Kibi region. * Drawstring bag made of silk However, silk was not produced in the Kinai region until the 4th century. * Tiled earthenware (Pottery fragments were excavated in 1996 (Heisei 8). Analyses of the composition of the clay components confirmed in 2001 that the pottery was unique in Japan, and that it was made using techniques from the {{ill|Korea|en|Korea|WD=Q18097|lt=Korea|1=Korea}}. * A miniature boat * Wooden arrowheads * Iwami-type shield-shaped wooden wares * a large number of imported pottery (exotic pottery).
However, there is a lack of conclusive evidence to date the site, such as the absence of bronze mirrors, swords, jade beads and iron objects, so it is not possible to say definitively that this was the site of the Yamatai Kingdom. {| cellpadding="0" border="0" style="float:right; border:2px solid #cccfff" |+'''Proportion of the area of origin of the pottery brought in''' |Ise and Tokai region !49% |- |Hokuriku and San-in region !17% |- |Kawachi region !10% |- |Kibi region !7% |- |Omi region !5% |- |Kanto region !5% |- |Harima region !3% |- |Western Seto Inland Sea region !3% |- |Kii region !1% |}
{{ill|Artifact (archaeology)|en|Artifact (archaeology)|WD=Q220659|lt=burial goods|1=Artifact (archaeology)}} have been unearthed from all over Japan, but most of them were made in {{ill|Ise Province|en|Ise Province|WD=Q864166|lt=Ise Province|1=Ise Province}}, which is adjacent to {{ill|Yamato Province|en|Yamato Province|WD=Q907495|lt=Yamato Province|1=Yamato Province}} and has had a close relationship with the country since ancient times. {{ill|Ise Province|en|Ise Province|WD=Q864166|lt=Ise Province|1=Ise Province}}, which was adjacent to {{ill|Yamato Province|en|Yamato Province|WD=Q907495|lt=Yamato Province|1=Yamato Province}} and had close relations with {{ill|Ise Bay|en|Ise Bay|WD=Q1368308|lt=Ise Bay|1=Ise Bay}}, and {{ill|Owari Province|en|Owari Province|WD=Q514506|lt=Owari Province|1=Owari Province}}, which is located to the east across {{ill|Ise Bay|en|Ise Bay|WD=Q1368308|lt=Ise Bay|1=Ise Bay}}. In addition to the pottery brought in, there is a large amount of pottery that was made in Yamato but is said to have regional characteristics, and the proportion of such pottery is higher at {{ill|Festival|en|Festival|WD=Q132241|lt=Ritual|1=Festival}}-related sites (30% of all pottery excavated at many sites). In addition, although these exotic pottery and artifacts are found from [[Kyushu]] to {{ill|Kantō region|en|Kantō region|WD=Q132480|lt=Kanto|1=Kantō region}} and the {{ill|Sea of Japan|en|Sea of Japan|WD=Q27092|lt=Sea of Japan|1=Sea of Japan}} side, there is very little pottery of Kyushu or Korean origin, suggesting that this site had little trade with the continent.<ref name="ishino2" /><ref name="tera2" /><gallery> File:纒向遺跡出土 土器群.JPG| part_of of excavated earthenware </gallery>
=== The main tombs of the Makimuku site ===
* [[Makimuku Ishizuka Kofun]] * {{ill|Makimuku Katsuyama Kofun|en|Makimuku Katsuyama Kofun|WD=Q11608502|lt=Makimuku Katsuyama Kofun|1=Makimuku Katsuyama Kofun}} * {{ill|Makimuku Yazuka Kofun|en|Makimuku Yazuka Kofun|WD=Q11608503|lt=Makimuku Yazuka Kofun|1=Makimuku Yatsuka Kofun}} * {{ill|Higashida Ōtsuka Kofun|en|Higashida Ōtsuka Kofun|WD=Q11528075|lt=Higaida-ōtsuka Kofun|1=Higaida Ōtsuka Kofun}} * [[Hokenoyama Kofun]] * {{ill|Hashihaka Kofun|en|Hashihaka Kofun|WD=Q11603420|lt=Hashihaka Kofun|1=Hashihaka Kofun}} === A peculiar site ===
* Although the site is said to be a large settlement, the remains of an inhabited settlement have not been found. All that can be seen today are ritual buildings, earthen mounds, ritual implements such as arcane discs and chicken-shaped wooden products, and large and small ditches (canals) protected by cypress sheet piles for distribution. Many scholars believe that the site was not a residential area, but rather a place for frequent gatherings of people and goods, and for rituals to {{ill|Mount Miwa|en|Mount Miwa|WD=Q860627|lt=Mount Miwa|1=Mount Miwa}} around the {{ill|Hashihaka Kofun|en|Hashihaka Kofun|WD=Q11603420|lt=Hashihaka Kofun|1=Hashihaka Kofun}}. * In the Tsuji/Torii-mae area, a 2 × 3 m long {{ill|Post in ground|en|Post in ground|WD=Q1695743|lt=digout pillar building|1=Post in ground}} and a row of fences running east–west to the south of it have been found; in the Ota Minami Tobizuka area, the remains of a collapsed house have been found; and in the Makinochi Ietsura area, a small 1 × 1 m long house and a 2 × 2 m long building with full columns have been found. In addition, 17 dugout pillar buildings have been found in the Ota Meguri area, and pit dwelling remains have been found in the Higashida Kakinoki and Ota Tobizuka areas. * According to Hironobu Ishino, this is "a large settlement site that suddenly appeared at the end of the 2nd century and suddenly disappeared in the middle of the 4th century".<ref name="ishino2" />。
=== Excavation Report ===
* [[:ja:石野博信|Ishino Hironobu]], [[:ja:関川尚功|Sekikawa Naokoh]], "Garments," Sakurai City Board of Education, September 1976. * [[:ja:関川尚功|Sekikawa, Naokoh]] and Matsunaga, Hiroaki, "Summary of Excavations at the Garoshi Site," The Archaeological Institute of Kashihara, 1984. * Naokoh Sekikawa and Hiroaki Matsunaga, "An Overview of the Excavation of the Garoshi Archaeological Site," The Archaeological Institute of Kashihara, Nara Prefecture, 1985. * [https://sitereports.nabunken.go.jp/62709 "Report on the Excavation of the Makimuku Site", Sakurai Municipal Archaeological Center, Excavation Report 28, 2007]. * [https://sitereports.nabunken.go.jp/62743 "Makimuku Ruins", Sakurai City Board of Education, Education Division, 1981]. * [https://sitereports.nabunken.go.jp/ja/53677 "Sakurai City Excavation Report by the National Treasury Subsidy in 2015", Sakurai Municipal Archaeological Heritage Excavation Report 46, 2017].
== Characteristics of the site ==
* The site dates from the late Yayoi period to the early {{ill|Kofun period|en|Kofun period|WD=Q459939|lt=Kofun period|1=Kofun period}}. * It is one of the largest settlement sites of its time, covering a vast area. * The {{ill|Hashihaka Kofun|en|Hashihaka Kofun|WD=Q11603420|lt=Hashihaka Kofun|1=Hashihaka Kofun}}, which has {{ill|Folklore|en|Folklore|WD=Q36192|lt=Tradition|1=Folklore}} as the tomb of [[Himiko]], is a huge 280-metre-long mound. The preceding mound, the Makimuku-type post-frontal-yen mound, with a mound length of around 90 m, is also the largest mound in the Japanese archipelago in the 3rd century, and is the first great royal tomb of the [[:en:Yamato Kingdom|Yamato Kingship]]. It is thought that the two tombs were politically linked, as they were also built in other parts of Japan. * {{ill|Himiko|en|Himiko|WD=Q234451|lt=Himiko|1=Himiko}}, the queen of the Yamataikoku Kingdom, according to one theory.
: Kazuo Higo introduces the view of Shinya Kasai in the {{ill|Taishō era|en|Taishō era|WD=Q329174|lt=Taisho|1=Taishō era}} period.<ref>{{Cite web|title=肥後和男『邪馬台国は大和である (1971st year )』 – 邪馬台国畿内説 卑弥呼はヤマトトモモソヒメ|url=https://www.buccyake-kojiki.com/archives/1016925732.html|access-date=2022-02-01|website=神社と古事記|language=ja}}</ref>。According to it, Kasai assigned Himiko to Momosohime, and her brother {{ill|Emperor Sujin|en|Emperor Sujin|WD=Q333530|lt=Emperor Sujin|1=Emperor Sujin}} to {{ill|Emperor Sujin|en|Emperor Sujin|WD=Q333530|lt=Emperor Sujin|1=Emperor Sujin}}. The rationale for this is as follows. :# Emperor Sujin's year of death in the Chinese zodiac was Boshin, close to the year of Himiko's death. :# It is clear that Himiko was a kind of priestess from the legend of her marriage to the deity of Mt. Miwa, and from the story of Nichiya Hitosaku, Yaya Kamisaku. She was the aunt of Emperor Sojin, but from the point of view of a foreigner (Chen Shou), she could be forgiven for being as wrong as his nephew and brother.
: Although there are many skeptics of this theory, some archaeologists believe that it is not unnatural for the Hashihaka Tomb to be Himiko's tomb, as the oldest giant anterior-posterior mound is the Hashihaka Tomb (the view of Shiraishi Taichiro and others).<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Shiraishi|first1=Taichirō|url=https://www.worldcat.org/oclc/45330682|title=Kofun to yamato seiken : kodai kokka wa ikani keisei sareta ka|last2=白石太一郎|date=1999|publisher=Bungei Shunjū|isbn=4-16-660036-2|location=Tōkyō|oclc=45330682}}</ref>。On the other hand, the size of the posterior circle of the {{ill|Hashihaka Kofun|en|Hashihaka Kofun|WD=Q11603420|lt=Hashihaka Kofun|1=Hashihaka Kofun}}, which is about 160m in diameter, may not match the description of Himiko's tomb in the {{ill|Wajinden|en|Wajinden|WD=Q1135798|lt=Wajinden|1=Wajinden}}. It is written in {{ill|Wajinden|en|Wajinden|WD=Q1135798|lt=Wajinden|1=Wajinden}} that "Heimyako died in a large tomb, which is about a hundred paces away from the tomb", which means that the size of the tomb is about 30m in the case of the short ri used in {{ill|Wajinden|en|Wajinden|WD=Q1135798|lt=Wajinden|1=Wajinden}}, which means that the Hashihaka Tomb is too big. Furthermore, the size of the Kofun was described in terms of diameter in the Wei Shi Wajin Den, so it is thought to be a round Kofun or similar. Therefore, there is a question mark over the use of the Hashihaka Tomb as the tomb of Himiko. (However, there is a theory that the front part of the tomb was additionally constructed in later times.)
* In 2013, more than 100 postholes were found in a building that is believed to have been constructed in the 3rd century. It is thought that the building was built and demolished many times.<ref>[http://sankei.jp.msn.com/life/news/130202/art13020213480002-n1.htm 卑弥呼の祭祀用建物跡？奈良・纒向遺跡で柱穴１００個超出土] 産経新聞 2013rd year 2月2日</ref>。 * Although pottery was brought in throughout the 3rd century, about 15% of the total excavated {{ill|pottery|en|pottery|WD=Q11642|lt=earthenware|1=Pottery}} is made up of pottery brought in from Suruga, Owari, Ise, Omi, Hokuriku, San'in, Kibi and other areas, but there is little pottery from northern Kyushu. The proportion of ritual-related remains is about 30%, but there are very few bronze mirrors and swords, which indicate exchange with the continent. This suggests that at that time there was a local royal power in this area which had little to do with Kitakyushu or the continent. * There are no Han mirrors, later Han mirrors or swords found at this site to prove that Himiko {{ill|Cao Wei|en|Cao Wei|WD=Q320930|lt=Cao Wei|1=Cao Wei}} and others interacted with the continent. In addition, no iron arrowheads were excavated. According to [[:ja:関川尚功|Sekikawa Naokoh]], "According to the Book of Wei, Himiko frequently sent messengers to Wei, and from Wei also came messengers and soldiers, so there was active exchange with the peninsula and the continent. Therefore, the active exchange with the peninsula and Korea as shown in the Heian-period Japanese history has not been proven and the site is not the site of the {{ill|Yamatai|en|Yamatai|WD=Q844295|lt=Yamatai|1=Yamatai}}.<ref>財団法人古代学協会、関川尚功（せきがわ ひさよし）邪馬台国と箸墓古墳</ref>。
=== The Royal Capital of the Yamato Kingdom === Kaoru Terasawa, in his book "The Birth of the Yamato Kingdom: The Royal Capital, the Makimuku Site and its Kofun Tombs", lists six features and peculiarities of the Makimuku Site<ref name="tera2">{{Cite book|url=https://www.worldcat.org/oclc/74978499|title=Nihon no kōkogaku : Doitsu ten kinen gaisetsu = Japans Archäologie und Geschichte bis zu den ersten Kaisern|version=2006 printing |publisher=Gakuseisha|others=Takashi Inada, 稲田孝司, Nara Bunkazai Kenkyūjo, 奈良文化財研究所.|isbn=4-311-75034-X|location=Tōkyō|oclc=74978499}}</ref>。
# It appeared suddenly at the beginning of the 3rd century. It is a very well planned settlement and large in size. # The site is the largest in the Japanese archipelago and had a municipal function. The site was the largest in the Japanese archipelago and had a municipal function. # There are few domestic utensils and civil engineering tools are conspicuous, and a huge canal was built and large-scale civil engineering works for city construction were carried out. # Water-conducting facilities and ritual facilities are royal rituals. Royalty-related buildings. Arcuate designs originating from the royal tombs of Kibi, special vessel bases and jars. # The {{ill|Hashihaka Kofun|en|Hashihaka Kofun|WD=Q11603420|lt=Hashihaka Kofun|1=Hashihaka Kofun}}, which was stylised on the edge of the habitation space, and the garnet-shaped posterior frontal Kofun that preceded it. # Ironware production. (No ironware has been found at the Garoshi site).
In addition, there is a pottery with "Oichi" written in ink from the early Heian period, and this site is considered to correspond to the "Ohoichi" township described in "[[Wamyō Ruijushō]]". '''{{ill|Shinto texts|en|Shinto texts|WD=Q11588760|lt=Kiki|1=Shinto texts}}'''", it is known that the city had a municipal function until later times, and furthermore, the {{ill|Emperor Suinin|en|Emperor Suinin|WD=Q314850|lt=Emperor Suinin|1=Emperor Suinin}} and {{ill|Emperor Keikō|en|Emperor Keikō|WD=Q329723|lt=Emperor Keikō|1=Emperor Keikō}}'s Shiki-no-mizukaki-no-miya, {{ill|Emperor Suinin|en|Emperor Suinin|WD=Q314850|lt=Emperor Suinin|1=Emperor Suinin}}, and {{ill|Emperor Keikō|en|Emperor Keikō|WD=Q329723|lt=Tamaki-no-Hishiro-no-Miya|1=Emperor Keikō}}, {{ill|Folklore|en|Folklore|WD=Q36192|lt=Folklore|1=Folklore}} are described as having existed.<ref name="tera2" />。
After saying this, Terasawa concluded, "There is no other huge settlement in the Japanese archipelago in the third century that has such a total of archaeological and philological features. Therefore, it is highly probable that the third-century site of Gengen was the city where the capital palace of the first kingship of the archipelago, called the {{ill|Yamato Kingship|en|Yamato Kingship|WD=Q2658252|lt=Yamato Kingdom|1=Yamato Kingship}}, was located".
Hironobu Ishino also argues that it was not a naturally occurring village but an artificially built city, based on the discovery of a large ditch and a ritual site with a seawall leading to the Yamato River, the unusually large number of pottery artifacts from outside the Kinki region, and the fact that at least one out of every five people at Gengen is estimated to have come from outside the Yamato region.<ref name="ishino2" />。
The following remarks also reinforce the view that the site is the birthplace of the {{ill|Yamato Kingship|en|Yamato Kingship|WD=Q2658252|lt=Yamato Kingship|1=Yamato Kingship}} or the royal capital of the {{ill|Yamato Kingship|en|Yamato Kingship|WD=Q2658252|lt=Yamato Kingship|1=Yamato Kingship}}.
* In the surrounding area, there are also palaces such as Nagase Asakura Palace of {{ill|Emperor Yūryaku|en|Emperor Yūryaku|WD=Q357235|lt=Emperor Yūryaku|1=Emperor Yūryaku}} in the 5th century, and Shiki (Isogi) Shima Omiya (Kinshiku) Palace of {{ill|Emperor Kinmei|en|Emperor Kinmei|WD=Q329792|lt=Kinmei|1=Emperor Kinmei}} in the 6th century. * The [[:en:Man'yoshu|Man'yoshu]] also contains many poems about the place name.
=== Birthplace of the Zenpokoenfun === [[File:Hashihaka_kohun_aerial.jpg|link=https://ja.Wikipedia.org/wiki/%E3%83%95%E3%82%A1%E3%82%A4%E3%83%AB:Hashihaka_kohun_aerial.jpg|right|thumb|240x240px|{{ill|Hashihaka Kofun|en|Hashihaka Kofun|WD=Q11603420|lt=Hashihaka Kofun|1=Hashihaka Kofun}}]] The {{ill|Hashihaka Kofun|en|Hashihaka Kofun|WD=Q11603420|lt=Hashihaka Kofun|1=Hashihaka Kofun}} located at the site is generally considered to be the beginning of the stylized {{ill|Kofun system|en|Kofun system|WD=Q11397224|lt=Zenpokoenfun system|1=Keyhole tomb order}}. Kaoru Terasawa considers the tombs belonging to the Makimukushizuka tumulus that preceded the {{ill|Hashihaka Kofun|en|Hashihaka Kofun|WD=Q11603420|lt=Hashihaka Kofun|1=Hashihaka Kofun}}, such as the Makimukushizuka tumulus, using the concept of "Makimukushizuka-type post-frontal-round tumulus", and places them in the emergence-period tumulus<ref>寺沢薫 「纒向型前方後円墳の築造」 同志社大学考古学シリーズIV『考古学と技術』同志社大学考古学シリーズ刊行会、1988th year 。</ref>。
Katsuyama Kofun is a [[scallop-shaped kofun]] with some elements indicating it was tranditional between that type and later {{ill|Zenpokoenfun|en|Zenpokoenfun|WD=Q11268718|lt=Zenpokoenfun|1=Zenpōkōenfun}}.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Kidder |first=J. Edward |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1515/9780824862848 |title=Himiko and Japan's Elusive Chiefdom of Yamatai |date=18 December 2017 |publisher=University of Hawaii Press |isbn=978-0-8248-6284-8}}</ref>{{ill|Zenpokoenfun|en|Zenpokoenfun|WD=Q11268718|lt={{rp|249}}}}
